title: Long-term banking of transplantable human organs

concept.text: Proposed capability: preserve whole human organs at cryogenic temperatures for months or years, then recover them safely for transplantation with durable function. A useful organ bank would preserve the organ’s coordinated biological function, including its blood vessels and tissue architecture, rather than merely keeping some cells alive. The innovation encompasses preservation, storage, recovery and validation after transplantation.

Technical synthesis from the supplied research: the proposed approach must control ice formation, deliver and remove protective chemicals, and manage cooling and warming throughout an entire organ. Vitrification aims to place tissue into a glass-like state without damaging ice formation; successful recovery then requires warming that avoids both ice formation and excessive temperature differences. These mechanisms explain the intended capability, but the retained source provides no inspectable scientific text confirming their implementation or performance in the cited experiment.

significance.text: Conditional impact synthesis: if organs could be stored for months or years and reliably recovered, transplantation could become a more deliberately scheduled process. Longer preservation would relax deadlines for assessment, recipient matching, transport and surgery, potentially allowing organs to reach suitable recipients who could not be served within a short preservation window. The revolutionary change would be the separation of organ availability from the immediate timing of transplantation.

Possible downstream benefits include more flexible distribution and time to coordinate clinical teams and recipient preparation. These are consequences that the proposed capability could enable, not demonstrated improvements in utilization, survival or access. Organ banking would not itself manufacture additional organs, prevent immune rejection or guarantee equitable allocation. Its practical impact would depend on recovery success, costs, infrastructure and how allocation systems use the additional time.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is reliable recovery of a whole human organ after prolonged cryogenic storage, followed by durable transplant function. The supplied research identifies ice formation, uneven warming, thermal cracking and cryoprotectant toxicity as key barriers. As a technical synthesis, these problems interact: a protective formulation and temperature schedule must prevent physical damage while remaining tolerable to the organ’s different tissues. The supplied evidence does not establish which combination solves these problems at human-organ scale.

Engineering synthesis: preservation must work throughout the organ, including regions that receive protective chemicals or heat less uniformly. Cooling and warming must avoid damaging temperature gradients, while cryoprotectant delivery and removal must avoid excessive chemical exposure. Scaling a successful process therefore requires more than increasing the size of a storage container; it requires control of transport, temperature and tissue injury across the organ.

A further barrier is demonstrating that apparent recovery predicts sustained biological performance. Reperfusion, laboratory measurements or immediate urine production, if established, would answer narrower questions than prolonged life-supporting function after transplantation. A kidney result would also leave open whether the same approach works for other organ types, whose structures, functions and vulnerabilities differ.

current_state.text: The supplied research and source index identify an item titled “Functional recovery of vitrified and nanowarmed human-scale pig kidneys,” attributed in the research to Zonghu Han and colleagues as a bioRxiv preprint dated 14 October 2026, with DOI 10.64898/2026.10.07.756990. However, the validated review reports that the retained PubMed copy contains only a cookie-access message. Neither an abstract nor full scientific text was available in that copy, so the document’s identity, publication details and experimental findings were not independently confirmed from its content.

The research attributes storage for up to one year, recovery during perfusion and immediate urine production after transplantation to that item. These quantitative and functional claims remain unverified because the retained copy contains no experimental results. The earlier statement that the review inspected the abstract is incorrect. The research also describes the work as not peer reviewed, but its peer-review status at the 1 November 2026 cutoff cannot be established from the supplied inspection material. This access limitation does not show that the reported findings are false.

Interpretive synthesis: even if the attributed observations are confirmed, human-scale pig kidneys would demonstrate an animal-organ result at a relevant size, rather than clinical preservation of human organs. Immediate post-transplant urine production would be an acute functional observation, rather than proof of durable life-supporting graft function. No demonstrated achievement can be independently established from the retained scientific content, and the empty supplied freshness record prevents a reliable account of developments through the stated cutoff.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: bank several human organ types for months or longer, recover them using defined procedures, and transplant them in controlled clinical studies. Long-term patient and graft outcomes should be comparable to appropriately matched conventionally preserved organs. These are proposed criteria for this record, not established consensus standards; a clinical protocol would need to specify follow-up duration, endpoints, acceptable comparability margins and matching variables.
completion_criteria.label: Human organs banked for months achieve comparable long-term transplant outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: repeat successful preservation and recovery across multiple organs and donors, with independent replication or validation across centers. Report failures and exclusions as well as successes, and relate outcomes to storage duration, organ condition and the recovery procedure. Demonstrations should establish sustained organ-specific function and graft survival rather than relying solely on appearance, perfusion measurements or immediate post-transplant activity.
completion_criteria.label: Independently validated banking reproducibly sustains organ function and graft survival

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: validate an end-to-end banking process that includes preparation, storage, transport, recovery and release for transplantation. Define the supported organ types, sizes, starting conditions, storage durations and handling tolerances. Results within these boundaries would establish demonstrated breadth; finite tests would not establish that every organ can be banked indefinitely or that a protocol transfers unchanged between organ types.
completion_criteria.label: End-to-end organ banking validated within explicitly defined practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BME-01, “Manufacturing transplantable human organs on demand,” addresses organ production, while BME-06 addresses preserving organs after they become available. The capabilities could complement each other by allowing manufactured organs to be stored. BME-12, “Reliable, scalable animal-to-human organ transplantation,” addresses a different source of organs and the challenges of transplantation across species. Banking could support its logistics, but recovery of a pig kidney would not by itself demonstrate safe animal-to-human transplantation.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-08, “Reliable, antigen-specific immune tolerance,” concerns the recipient’s immune response. Successful banking would still leave rejection prevention unresolved. BME-13, “Durable autonomous artificial-organ replacement,” concerns engineered substitutes for organ function; BME-06 instead seeks to retain and recover the function of a biological organ.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-14, “Shelf-stable, broadly compatible replacement for critical blood functions,” shares the ambition of making biological support available when needed. Its replacement product and compatibility goals differ from recovering a structurally intact organ after cryogenic storage. BME-11, “Controlled regeneration of complex organs in the adult body,” and BME-17, “Minimally invasive assembly of functional tissue inside the body,” concern creating or rebuilding tissue in the recipient rather than storing an organ outside the body.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-10, “Validated patient-specific models for testing treatments before use,” could complement banking by informing assessment or treatment choices during a longer planning window. Such models would address prediction, while organ banking must demonstrate actual preservation and transplant function. These relationships preserve the concepts as distinct innovations with different completion requirements.

unresolved_issues: The intended document’s identity and scientific contents remain unconfirmed from the retained artifact; an accessible abstract or full text is needed to assess the attributed findings.
Storage for up to one year, perfusion recovery and immediate post-transplant urine production remain unverified, including their experimental conditions, sample sizes and failure rates.
The supplied material does not establish durable life-supporting transplant function or clinical preservation of human organs.
Publication details and peer-review status at the 1 November 2026 cutoff remain unverified.
The empty freshness record prevents an assessment of developments through the cutoff or whether the capability remained unsolved at that date.
The scope and severity of the stated organ-scale barriers lack inspectable scientific support in the supplied evidence.
Clinical follow-up duration, outcome endpoints, comparability margins, matching variables and practical storage and distribution limits remain to be defined.

brief.title: Human organs stored for later transplantation
possible: A donated organ could wait for the patient who needs it. Hospitals could store whole human organs for months or years, then recover them for transplantation with lasting function. Patients and clinical teams could prepare for planned surgery instead of racing against a short preservation window.
why: More time would let transplant teams assess organs, find suitable recipients and arrange transport. Organs could reach patients who cannot be served within today's short deadlines, separating the moment an organ becomes available from the moment it must be transplanted.

sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reported recovery of pig kidneys the size of human kidneys after storage for up to a year. They showed blood vessel function and urine production, including immediately after transplantation.
sources.quote: Rewarmed kidneys demonstrated vascular, metabolic and excretory function during normothermic perfusion, with limited histological injury, and reperfused homogeneously and produced urine immediately after transplantation.
sources.cited_for: Recovery after prolonged storage is possible in animal kidneys at a size relevant to human transplantation.
sources.not_established: Immediate urine production does not establish lasting, life-supporting transplant function or successful banking of human organs.

sources.who: Zonghu Han, Joseph Sushil Rao and colleagues
sources.showed: Rat kidneys stored for up to 100 days recovered after warming and sustained recipients whose own kidneys had been removed. The process used ice-free cooling and tiny magnetic particles to warm the organs from within.
sources.quote:
Full
renal function was restored after nanowarming and transplantation,
with the transplanted organs sustaining the life of the recipient
animals.
sources.cited_for: A stored whole organ can recover enough function to sustain life after transplantation.
sources.not_established: Success in rat kidneys does not establish comparable long-term outcomes in human organs or independent replication across centers.

sources.showed: A rabbit survived with a kidney cooled into an ice-free, glass-like state and then transplanted back. This was an isolated success, with impaired kidney function and only brief storage at the lowest temperatures.
sources.quote:
During the removal of M22, the kidney perfused nor-
mally, and during transplantation, the urine was not bloody and
the kidney appearance was reasonable and seemed to be recover-
ing at closure.
sources.cited_for: An early animal experiment established that an organ could support life after ice-free cooling and recovery.
sources.not_established: An isolated success after brief storage does not establish reliable recovery after prolonged banking.

sources.who: Anirudh Sharma, Charles Y. Lee and colleagues
sources.showed: Rat livers recovered after ice-free cooling and warming from within using tiny magnetic particles. They retained tissue structure and produced bile during warm fluid circulation, but showed signs of injury and impaired waste removal.
sources.quote: This study demonstrates the ability to load rat livers with both CPA and sIONPs by vascular perfusion, cool them rapidly to an ice-free vitrified state, and rapidly and homogenously rewarm them.
sources.cited_for: Whole-organ preservation has shown partial functional recovery beyond kidneys.
sources.not_established: Function during warm fluid circulation does not establish life-supporting liver function after transplantation.

sources.showed: Rat hearts were cooled into an ice-free state and rewarmed without cracking. They retained tissue structure and showed preliminary electrical activity, but protective chemicals still caused injury.
sources.quote:
Here, using a rat heart model, controlled machine perfusion loading and 
unloading of CPA and sIONPs, cooling to a vitrified state, and fast and 
uniform nanowarming without crystallization or cracking is demonstrated.
sources.cited_for: Rapid, even warming can prevent physical damage in whole rat hearts.
sources.not_established: Electrical activity and intact tissue do not establish that a recovered heart can pump enough blood to sustain a transplant recipient.

shown: Zonghu Han, Joseph Sushil Rao and colleagues recovered stored rat kidneys that sustained transplant recipients for 30 days without their own kidneys. They used vitrification, cooling into an ice-free glass-like state, and nanowarming, heating tiny magnetic particles inside the organ.

Han and colleagues also reported recovery of human-sized pig kidneys after storage for up to a year, with urine production immediately after transplantation. That work is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. It does not demonstrate lasting transplant function.
missing: Whole human organs have yet to recover from prolonged storage and deliver lasting transplant outcomes comparable to conventional preservation.
Protective chemicals and temperature control must prevent ice, cracking and chemical injury throughout human-sized organs.
Independent teams have yet to demonstrate reliable banking across donors and organ types, including preparation, transport and recovery.

milestones.label: Banked human organs achieve comparable long-term transplant outcomes
milestones.explanation: Controlled clinical studies would have to show comparable long-term patient and transplanted-organ outcomes across several human organ types stored for months. This would establish clinical usefulness.

milestones.label: Independent validation confirms reproducible organ function and transplant survival
milestones.explanation: Repeated preservation across organs and donors would have to sustain function and transplanted-organ survival, with independent validation and failures reported. This would establish reliability beyond isolated successes.

milestones.label: The complete banking process works within defined practical limits
milestones.explanation: Preparation, storage, transport and recovery would have to work within defined limits for organ type, size, condition, storage time and handling. This would establish where the complete process can be used reliably.

uncertain: The follow-up period and acceptable differences from conventional transplant outcomes still need to be defined.
It remains unclear how well success in kidneys will transfer to organs with different structures and vulnerabilities.
The effects of storage duration, donor organ condition and recovery procedures on failure rates remain unresolved.

page.title: Cryogenic banking of transplantable human organs
page.definition: Whole human organs can be stored at cryogenic temperatures for a month or longer, rewarmed and transplanted with life-supporting function. Vitrification, one approach, cools an organ into an ice-free, glass-like state.

goal.need: HRSA's usual preservation interval for a donor heart is one-sixth of that for a donor kidney. Heart and liver recipients are usually identified before organ recovery. Organ banking seeks to extend the interval available for recipient matching, assessment and transport.

figures.caption: Usual intervals from organ removal to transplantation

statements.context: A milestone in the developer's published roadmap for bringing cryopreserved donor organs into clinical use.

completion.title: A human organ supports a recipient after at least one month of cryogenic banking.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed clinical report demonstrates that a whole human organ was stored at cryogenic temperatures for at least 1 calendar month, rewarmed, transplanted into a living recipient and provided life-supporting organ function through the reported clinical follow-up. Immediate reperfusion or urine production alone is insufficient. The cited roadmaps establish no numerical follow-up duration or comparison margin.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; the one-month minimum is an Atlas criterion, not a published clinical acceptance threshold.
completion.basis: Searched Organ Preservation Alliance and Until roadmaps, ATP-Bio targets, FDA material and ClinicalTrials.gov for a test combining months-long cryogenic storage with human graft survival; none was located. The roadmaps set clinical transplantation goals without operational endpoints. The one-month floor is informed by the Alliance's separate 1-month-to-2-year target for warmer subzero storage.

milestones.title: A small-mammal whole organ retains function after vitrification and rewarming.
milestones.criterion: Vitrify and rewarm a small-mammal whole organ with retained organ-level function; the roadmap gives no numerical recovery cutoff. The 2023 rat-liver paper reports bile production during warm perfusion, with impaired dye excretion; its accessible abstract omits sample sizes. Rat-heart optical mapping found electrical activity in 3 nanowarmed hearts versus 3 controls in a paper published on 1 October 2021. These results do not establish life-supporting transplantation.
milestones.set_by: Organ Preservation Alliance, Beta Roadmap Report, printed page 34; small-mammal recovery criterion appears in a table.

milestones.title: A cryopreserved whole organ recovers full function in a preclinical model.
milestones.criterion: Recover full organ function after cryopreservation in a preclinical model; Until gives no numerical recovery cutoff. On 9 June 2023, Han and colleagues reported rat kidneys stored for 1–100 days at −150 °C: 5/5 recipients lacking both native kidneys survived the 30-day follow-up, and renal function normalized after 2–3 weeks. Five fresh-graft controls also survived. This establishes the kidney result for the animal model and follow-up studied.
milestones.set_by: Until, Roadmap, Organs section; a developer's published criterion, not a field-wide consensus.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate full organ function post-cryopreservation in preclinical models.

milestones.title: A large-mammal organ retains pre-transplant function after vitrification and rewarming.
milestones.criterion: Vitrify and rewarm a large-mammal organ with healthy pre-transplant functionality; the roadmap supplies no acceptance range or replication count. A preprint posted on 14 October 2026 reports pig kidneys recovered after storage at −150 °C for up to one year, with vascular, metabolic and excretory function during warm perfusion and immediate urine production after transplantation. It is not peer reviewed; its accessible abstract supplies no sample sizes or survival follow-up. This establishes partial recovery, not the roadmap's healthy-function criterion.
milestones.set_by: Organ Preservation Alliance, Beta Roadmap Report, printed page 35; large-mammal recovery criterion appears in a table.

milestones.title: A regulator authorizes a first-in-human study of whole-organ cryopreservation.
milestones.criterion: Obtain regulatory authorization to begin a first-in-human study of organ cryopreservation. Until's roadmap specifies no jurisdiction, sample size or endpoints. No corresponding authorization or registered human whole-organ cryopreservation transplantation study was located.
milestones.set_by: Until, Roadmap, Organs section; regulatory authorization is the developer's stated milestone.
milestones.threshold_quote: Secure regulatory approval for first-in-human (FIH) trial for organ cryopreservation.

not_found: No operational human completion test combining a cryogenic storage interval with a graft-survival endpoint was located in the roadmap, FDA or ClinicalTrials.gov searches.
No registered human transplantation study or first-in-human authorization for cryogenically banked whole organs was located.
The pig-kidney preprint's full text returned HTTP 403; its accessible abstract omits sample sizes and survival follow-up.
The rat-liver full text returned a browser challenge; its accessible abstract gives no sample sizes.
